rationale: B wins because it finds the cleanest editor-sale in the update: "Whoop puts a cleared ECG and an uncleared blood-pressure estimate on the same wrist." That is a real regulatory split with a beat, a peg, and proof demands. A's best line, "Whoop's new blood-pressure number isn't a medical reading — and needs a cuff to even start," is strong, but it leaves the cleared-vs-wellness tension in pieces. B still needs editing; "What Whoop's cardiologists actually signed off on" overstates the advisory-board fact.
gaps_in_A: A misses the strongest combined frame: it splits "FDA-cleared ECG" and "non-medical 'wellness' estimate" into separate angles instead of making the regulatory contrast the lead story.
"screenless band" is not in the supplied update. It may be true of Whoop, but this exercise needs the angle grounded in the given facts or clearly marked as proof to obtain.
"the wearable was supposed to replace" overstates the blood-pressure fact. The update says cuff calibration is required; it does not say Whoop promised replacement.

"health features are increasingly paywalled" is a real possible trend, but A only has one company in the update. It correctly asks for more proof, but the trend claim should stay conditional until then.
gaps_in_B: "What Whoop's cardiologists actually signed off on" is the ugliest overreach in either set. The update says a cardiologist advisory board reviewed the features; review is not sign-off.
"what a privately held company last valued at $3.6B needs from parity to hold a subscription base" invents motive from valuation. That is boardroom fan fiction unless Whoop or analysts say it.
"false positives, worried-well referrals" is plausible clinical context, but it is not supplied. Keep it as a question for experts, not a premise the angle rests on.
"cleared medical screening feature" is close to the line. The safer wording is FDA-cleared AFib detection, because the exact indication matters here.
